title: State v. Puloka — Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law Excluding AI-Enhanced Video under Frye (First US Ruling on AI-Enhanced Video Admissibility)
pub: State v. Puloka, No. 21-1-04851-2 KNT (Wash. Super. Ct., King Cty. Mar. 29, 2024) (unreported)
author: Judge Leroy McCullough

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The ruling accepts the need for selective, use-context-specific deployment and materially extends it to courtroom evidence. It shows that AI enhancement may be unsuitable where opacity, non-reproducibility and generated image detail prevent reliable forensic evaluation, while distinguishing those methods from established, integrity-preserving techniques. Its case- and record-specific reasoning also supports continuous rather than categorical assessment.
qs: The Topaz Video AI enhancement tool(s), which utilize ‘machine learning’ algorithms, have not been peer-reviewed by the forensic video analysis community, are — at the present time — not reproducible by that community, and are not accepted generally in that community.

The video evidence produced by the Topaz Video AI enhancement model does not satisfy ER 401, as the resulting video does not show with integrity what actually happened but uses opaque methods to represent what the AI model ‘thinks’ should be shown.

mo.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control

kp.k: AI video enhancement required general acceptance under Frye
kp.d: The court found using AI tools to enhance video introduced in a criminal trial to be a novel technique. It therefore required the evidence's proponent to establish general acceptance of the methodology in the relevant scientific community, rather than asking the court to decide whether the underlying scientific theory was correct.
qs: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to enhance video introduced i in a criminal trial is a novel technique.
The standard for admitting evidence utilizing a novel scientific theory or principle is whether it has achieved general acceptance in the relevant scientific community.

kp.k: Forensic standards governed, not video production practices
kp.d: The defense urged the court to treat the video production community as the relevant community. The court instead selected forensic video analysis, crediting State expert Grant Fredericks' distinction between preserving image integrity and producing a smoother, more attractive video. Commercial production usage did not establish forensic acceptance.
qs: The scientific community relevant to this Court’s determination of the admissibility of videos enhanced by AI tools is the forensic video analysis community.
Fredericks’ focus in performing forensic video analysis is on ‘image integrity’, and not on creating a smoother, more attractive product for a user.

kp.k: Apparent clarity came with false and altered image details
kp.d: Defense witness Brian Racherbaeumer used Topaz Labs AI and further processing in Adobe Premier Pro to enhance a low-resolution source video with substantial motion blur. According to Fredericks' testimony, credited by the court, the AI tools added approximately sixteen times the original number of pixels and created false detail that changed portions of the video's meaning; objects no longer retained their original shapes and colors.
qs: According to Fredericks, the AI tool(s) utilized by Racherbaeumer added approximately sixteen times the number of pixels, compared to the number of pixels in the original images to enhance each video frame, utilizing an algorithm and enhancement method unknown to and unreviewed by any forensic video expert.

Furthermore, he demonstrated that the AI method created false image detail and that process is not acceptable to the forensic video community because it has the effect of changing the meaning of portions of the video.

kp.d: Fredericks demonstrated that processing both removed original information and introduced information absent from the source. The court found that artifact removal and shape alteration also prevented examination of reference, predictive and bi-directional frames, making accepted forensic analysis impossible for the proffered enhanced video.
qs: Mr. Fredericks explained and demonstrated that the AI process removed information that was in the original images and it added information that was not in the original images.
In short, the Al-enhancement tools made proper, accepted forensic analysis of the video impossible.

kp.k: Operator expertise did not establish AI reliability
kp.d: Racherbaeumer candidly acknowledged that he was a videographer and filmmaker rather than a forensically trained technician. He could not establish forensic-community use or reliability testing, did not know the models' training videos or whether their algorithms employed generative AI, and agreed that the algorithms were opaque and proprietary. These were limitations of the defense's evidentiary showing, not a finding that the software necessarily used generative AI.
qs: He was very candid and open about the fact that he is not — and has not claimed to be — a forensic video technician and has not been forensically trained.
He was unaware of any testing, publications, or discussion groups within his peer group that was involved in evaluating the reliability of AI tools for video enhancement purposes.
such models employ ‘generative AI’ in their algorithms, and agreed that such algorithms are opaque and proprietary.

kp.k: Peer review and reproducibility were absent
kp.d: The court concluded that the Topaz tools lacked forensic peer review, reproducibility and general acceptance at the time of the ruling. It found that any market testing by video producers could not be evaluated because testing outcomes were unpublished. The defense also supplied no appellate decisions or publications approving introduction of AI-enhanced video evidence.
qs: The Topaz Video AI enhancement tool(s), which utilize ‘machine learning’ algorithms, have not been peer-reviewed by the forensic video analysis community, are — at the present time — not reproducible by that community, and are not accepted generally in that community.
As a result, their findings, if they exist, cannot be evaluated by the defense expert, the © forensic video analysis community, or by this court.
The defense has not offered any articles, publications, or secondary legal sources approving the introduction of Al-enhanced video evidence in a criminal or civil trial.

kp.k: Established interpolation offered a contrasting evidentiary approach
kp.d: The findings contrasted opaque machine-learning enhancement with nearest-neighbor, bi-cubic and bi-linear enlargement, described as reproducible techniques used by forensic analysts for decades. The court quoted Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence guidance that nearest-neighbor interpolation may mitigate distortion of small objects, while reporting its warning about accurately replicating machine-learning interpolation processes.
qs: Utilizing Nearest Neighbor interpolation to enlarge imagery that contains small objects within (e.g., weapon in hands) may help mitigate the distortion of the object’s shape, length, or size represented by a few pixels.
The Nearest Neighbor algorithm can reduce the potential of providing a misleading representation of the level of pixel detail in the original imagery.
it can be challenging to identify what process were applied to the imagery and replicate those steps with accuracy.

kp.k: Relevance and prejudice independently weighed against admission
kp.d: The court concluded that the resulting video failed ER 401 because it did not faithfully show what happened. Under ER 403, it found that potential confusion, muddled eyewitness testimony and a time-consuming trial within a trial substantially outweighed any relevance. The risk was particularly significant because jurors would likely focus on the sizes and locations of people and objects.
qs: The video evidence produced by the Topaz Video AI enhancement model does not satisfy ER 401, as the resulting video does not show with integrity what actually happened but uses opaque methods to represent what the AI model ‘thinks’ should be shown.

The danger of unfair prejudice is particularly concerning in this case, as the jury will likely be focused on the size and location of individuals and objects during the events depicted by the Al-enhanced video:

kp.k: Court excluded enhanced exhibits while preserving source-video use
kp.d: The court refused the defense's enhanced Exhibit 2 and all AI-enhanced videos on Exhibit 5, which contained seven enhanced videos. It identified the approximately ten-second source recording as the best evidence for the jury. Both parties could use that recording, the defense acknowledged its other expert could base testimony on it, and the State intended to offer it alongside multiple eyewitnesses; the court therefore regarded enhanced-video testimony as noncrucial.
qs: The best evidence for the jury is the source video recorded and preserved in Exhibit 1.
Both sides can use the source video for argument, and the jury will be able to utilize the source video for its determination.
The Defense’s proffered pre-trial Exhibit 2 is refused, and all Al-enhanced videos on pre- trial Exhibit 5 are refused.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The court finds that the particular AI video enhancement introduced false detail, changed depicted objects, and prevented accepted forensic analysis, despite the defense witness's claim of improved visual clarity.
pts.d: Defense witness Brian Racherbaeumer described Topaz Labs AI as increasing resolution, sharpness, definition, and edge smoothness. Judge Leroy McCullough credited forensic video analyst Grant Fredericks's testimony that the processing added approximately sixteen times the original number of pixels, removed original information, added new information, and changed shapes and colors. These are findings about the proffered videos and processing, not a measured error rate for AI systems generally.

pts.k: The court treats AI enhancement of criminal-trial video as a novel technique requiring general acceptance in forensic video analysis and excludes the defense's enhanced exhibits.
pts.d: McCullough identifies the forensic video analysis community—not the broader video production community proposed by the defense—as the relevant community under Frye. He concludes that the Topaz tools lacked peer review, reproducibility, and general acceptance there. The court also finds that the resulting video fails ER 401 because it does not faithfully depict events, and independently identifies ER 403 prejudice concerns. The ruling excludes Exhibit 2 and all AI-enhanced videos on Exhibit 5; it does not announce a permanent prohibition on every form of AI evidence.

pts.k: The court predicts that admitting these enhanced videos would confuse the issues and eyewitness testimony and could generate a time-consuming subsidiary dispute about the AI process.
pts.d: McCullough's prospective trial-management and prejudice assessment concerns this case, where jurors would likely focus on the size and location of people and objects. He concludes that any relevance is substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice. This is a judicial assessment of anticipated consequences, not an empirical finding about actual jury behavior or trial duration.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The findings rest on expert testimony and demonstrations, the source and enhanced videos, professional guidance, and evidentiary authorities—not a systematic AI benchmark.
pts.d: The court heard both witnesses, reviewed briefing and exhibits, and expressly found Fredericks credible. Fredericks was a certified forensic video analyst with approximately 300 court appearances over ten years, divided roughly equally between prosecution/plaintiff and defense work. Racherbaeumer acknowledged lacking forensic training, knowledge of the training videos, and awareness of reliability testing within his peer group. Fredericks demonstrated altered image details and relied on the Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence's resizing guidance. The legal analysis cites Frye, Washington decisions, and evidence rules. The court records that the defense supplied no appellate decisions or publications approving admission; that is a statement about the record, not proof of an exhaustive search or of the document title's 'first US ruling' characterization.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The ruling assesses the tools and evidentiary record as of the February–March 2024 proceedings, explicitly qualifying the reproducibility finding as current.
pts.d: The court heard testimony on February 21–22, argument on February 26, and delivered an oral ruling on February 29; the supplied order is dated March 29, 2024. Racherbaeumer said the tool had been commercially available for about three years. The admissibility conclusion turns on novelty and lack of general acceptance in the relevant scientific community at that time. The anticipated trial harms are conditional on admitting the proffered enhanced footage. The court does not predict when these tools might become acceptable or make forecasts about legal employment, pricing, or markets.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate effects concern the defendant's presentation of evidence, both parties' experts and lawyers, forensic analysts, the jury, and the trial court.
pts.d: The defense cannot introduce the enhanced exhibits, but both sides retain access to the preserved source video for argument and expert use. The court notes that the defense's other retained expert could use that source and that the prosecution planned multiple eyewitnesses. Forensic analysts face loss of information necessary for accepted examination; jurors face potentially misleading depictions; the court anticipates confusion and additional litigation over processing. The source frames the enhanced evidence as unnecessary to determining the charges, rather than as indispensable evidence lost through exclusion.
